blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In our day to day life, we come across many queries such
as – What is your height? How should a football player hit
the ball to give a pass to another player of his team? Observe
that a possible answer to the first query may be 1.6 meters,
a quantity that involves only one value (magnitude) which
is a real number. Such quantities are called $scalars$.
However, an answer to the second query is a quantity (called
force) which involves muscular strength (magnitude) and
direction (in which another player is positioned). Such
quantities are called $vectors$. In mathematics, physics and
engineering, we frequently come across with both types of
quantities, namely, scalar quantities such as length, mass,
time, distance, speed, area, volume, temperature, work,
money, voltage, density, resistance etc. and vector quantities like displacement, velocity,
acceleration, force, weight, momentum, electric field intensity etc.

W.R. Hamilton
(1805-1865)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will study some of the basic concepts about vectors, various
operations on vectors, and their algebraic and geometric properties. These two type of
properties, when considered together give a full realisation to the concept of vectors,
and lead to their vital applicability in various areas as mentioned above.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.2 Some Basic Concepts

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let '$l$' be any straight line in plane or three dimensional space. This line can be given
two directions by means of arrowheads. A line with one of these directions prescribed
is called a $directed$ $line$ (Fig 10.1 (i), (ii)).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 10.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now observe that if we restrict the line $l$ to the line segment AB, then a magnitude
is prescribed on the line $l$ with one of the two directions, so that we obtain a $directed$
$line$ $segment$ (Fig 10.1(iii)). Thus, a directed line segment has magnitude as well as
direction.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Definition 1 A quantity that has magnitude as well as direction is called a vector.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Notice that a directed line segment is a vector (Fig 10.1(iii)), denoted as $\overline{\text{AB}}$ or
simply as $\vec{a}$, and read as ‘vector $\overline{\text{AB}}$’ or ‘vector $\vec{a}$’.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The point A from where the vector $\overline{\text{AB}}$ starts is called its *initial point*, and the
point B where it ends is called its *terminal point*. The distance between initial and
terminal points of a vector is called the *magnitude* (or length) of the vector, denoted as
$|\overline{\text{AB}}|$, or $|\vec{a}|$, or $a$. The arrow indicates the direction of the vector.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text: Note Since the length is never negative, the notation $|\vec{a}| < 0$ has no meaning.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Position Vector

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From Class XI, recall the three dimensional right handed rectangular coordinate system
(Fig 10.2(i)). Consider a point P in space, having coordinates $(x, y, z)$ with respect to
the origin O$(0, 0, 0)$. Then, the vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OP}}$ having O and P as its initial and terminal
points, respectively, is called the *position vector* of the point P with respect
to O. Using distance formula (from Class XI), the magnitude of $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OP}}$ (or $\vec{r}$) is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$|\overrightarrow{OP}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In practice, the position vectors of points A, B, C, etc., with respect to the origin O
are denoted by $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$, etc., respectively (Fig 10.2 (ii)).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 10.2

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Direction Cosines

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Consider the position vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OP}}$ (or $\vec{r}$) of a point $\mathrm{P}(x, y, z)$ as in Fig 10.3. The angles $\alpha$,
$\beta$, $\gamma$ made by the vector $\vec{r}$ with the positive directions of $x$, $y$ and $z$-axes respectively,
are called its *direction angles*. The cosine values of these angles, i.e., $\cos \alpha$, $\cos \beta$ and
$\cos \gamma$ are called *direction cosines* of the vector $\vec{r}$, and usually denoted by $l$, $m$ and $n$,
respectively.
$\mathbf{Z}$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 10.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From Fig 10.3, one may note that the triangle OAP is right angled, and in it, we
have $\cos \alpha = \frac{x}{r}$ ($r$ stands for $|\vec{r}|$). Similarly, from the right angled triangles OBP and
OCP, we may write $\cos \beta = \frac{y}{r}$ and $\cos \gamma = \frac{z}{r}$. Thus, the coordinates of the point P may
also be expressed as $(lr, mr, nr)$. The numbers $lr, mr$ and $nr$, proportional to the direction
cosines are called as $direction$ $ratios$ of vector $\vec{r}$, and denoted as $a, b$ and $c$, respectively.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text: Note One may note that $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$ but $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \neq 1$, in general.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.3 Types of Vectors

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Zero Vector** A vector whose initial and terminal points coincide, is called a zero vector
(or null vector), and denoted as $\vec{0}$. Zero vector can not be assigned a definite direction
as it has zero magnitude. Or, alternatively otherwise, it may be regarded as having any
direction. The vectors $\overrightarrow{AA}$, $\overrightarrow{BB}$ represent the zero vector,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Unit Vector** A vector whose magnitude is unity (i.e., 1 unit) is called a unit vector. The
unit vector in the direction of a given vector $\vec{a}$ is denoted by $\hat{a}$ .

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Coinitial Vectors** Two or more vectors having the same initial point are called coinitial
vectors.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Collinear Vectors** Two or more vectors are said to be collinear if they are parallel to
the same line, irrespective of their magnitudes and directions.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Equal Vectors** Two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are said to be equal, if they have the same
magnitude and direction regardless of the positions of their initial points, and written
as $\vec{a} = \vec{b}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Negative of a Vector** A vector whose magnitude is the same as that of a given vector
(say, $\overline{\text{AB}}$), but direction is opposite to that of it, is called *negative* of the given vector.
For example, vector $\overline{\text{BA}}$ is negative of the vector $\overline{\text{AB}}$, and written as $\overline{\text{BA}} = -\overline{\text{AB}}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\textit{\textbf{Remark}}$ The vectors defined above are such that any of them may be subject to its
parallel displacement without changing its magnitude and direction. Such vectors are
called $\textit{free vectors}$. Throughout this chapter, we will be dealing with free vectors only.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.4 Addition of Vectors

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A vector $\overline{\text{AB}}$ simply means the displacement from a point
A to the point B. Now consider a situation that a girl
moves from A to B and then from B to C
(Fig 10.7). The net displacement made by the girl from
point A to the point C, is given by the vector $\overline{\text{AC}}$ and
expressed as

$$ \overline{AC} = \overline{AB} + \overline{BC} $$

This is known as the \textit{triangle law of vector addition}.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 10.7

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In general, if we have two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ (Fig 10.8 (i)), then to add them, they are
positioned so that the initial point of one coincides with the terminal point of the other
(Fig 10.8(ii)).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 10.8

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For example, in Fig 10.8 (ii), we have shifted vector $\vec{b}$ without changing its magnitude
and direction, so that it's initial point coincides with the terminal point of $\vec{a}$. Then, the
vector $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$, represented by the third side AC of the triangle ABC, gives us the sum (or
resultant) of the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ i.e., in triangle ABC (Fig 10.8 (ii)), we have

$$ \overline{AB} + \overline{BC} = \overline{AC} $$

Now again, since $\overline{\mathrm{AC}} = -\overline{\mathrm{CA}}$, from the above equation, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} + \overrightarrow{CA} = \overrightarrow{AA} = \vec{0} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This means that when the sides of a triangle are taken in order, it leads to zero
resultant as the initial and terminal points get coincided (Fig 10.8(iii)).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, construct a vector $\overline{\text{BC}'}$ so that its magnitude is same as the vector $\overline{\text{BC}}$, but the
direction opposite to that of it (Fig 10.8 (iii)), i.e.,

$$\overrightarrow{BC'} = -\overline{BC}$$

Then, on applying triangle law from the Fig 10.8 (iii), we have

$$ \overline{\mathrm{AC}'} = \overline{\mathrm{AB}} + \overline{\mathrm{BC}'} = \overline{\mathrm{AB}} + (-\overline{\mathrm{BC}}) = \vec{a} - \vec{b} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The vector $\overline{\mathrm{AC}'}$ is said to represent the difference of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, consider a boat in a river going from one bank of the river to the other in a
direction perpendicular to the flow of the river. Then, it is acted upon by two velocity
vectors—one is the velocity imparted to the boat by its engine and other one is the
velocity of the flow of river water. Under the simultaneous influence of these two
velocities, the boat in actual starts travelling with a different velocity. To have a precise
idea about the effective speed and direction
(i.e., the resultant velocity) of the boat, we have
the following law of vector addition.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we have two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ represented
by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram
in magnitude and direction (Fig 10.9), then their
sum $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ is represented in magnitude and
direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram
through their common point. This is known as
the $parallelogram$ $law$ $of$ $vector$ $addition$.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig 10.9

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note From Fig 10.9, using the triangle law, one may note that
$$\overline{OA} + \overline{AC} = \overline{OC}$$
or $$\overline{OA} + \overline{OB} = \overline{OC} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{(since } \overline{AC} = \overline{OB} \text{ )}$$
which is parallelogram law. Thus, we may say that the two laws of vector
addition are equivalent to each other.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Properties of vector addition

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Property 1 For any two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$,

$$\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \vec{b} + \vec{a} \qquad \qquad \text{(Commutative property)}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Proof Consider the parallelogram ABCD
(Fig 10.10). Let $\overline{\text{AB}} = \vec{a}$ and $\overline{\text{BC}} = \vec{b}$, then using
the triangle law, from triangle ABC, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, since the opposite sides of a
parallelogram are equal and parallel, from
Fig 10.10, we have, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AD}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{BC}}=\vec{b}$ and
$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{DC}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}=\vec{a}$. Again using triangle law, from
triangle ADC, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{AC}} = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{AD}} + \overrightarrow{\mathrm{DC}} = \vec{b} + \vec{a} $$

Hence $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \vec{b} + \vec{a}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Property 2 For any three vectors $a, b$ and $c$

$$(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) + \vec{c} = \vec{a} + (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) \qquad \text{(Associative property)}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Proof Let the vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be represented by $\overline{\text{PQ}}$, $\overline{\text{QR}}$ and $\overline{\text{RS}}$, respectively, as
shown in Fig 10.11(i) and (ii).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Then $$\bar{a} + \bar{b} = \overline{\text{PQ}} + \overline{\text{QR}} = \overline{\text{PR}}$$
and $$\bar{b} + \bar{c} = \overline{\text{QR}} + \overline{\text{RS}} = \overline{\text{QS}}$$
So $$\bar{(a)} + \bar{(b)} + \bar{c} = \overline{\text{PR}} + \overline{\text{RS}} = \overline{\text{PS}}$$
flags: [translation_divergence] The Hindi edition has split the proof into extra equations T22 and T23 to show both sides of the associative property more explicitly, which makes the proof slightly clearer than the English side.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
and $\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \bar{a} + (\bar{b} + \bar{c}) = \overline{\text{PQ}} + \overline{\text{QS}} = \overline{\text{PS}}$
Hence $\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad (\bar{a} + \bar{b}) + \bar{c} = \bar{a} + (\bar{b} + \bar{c})$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
\textit{\textbf{Remark}} The associative property of vector addition enables us to write the sum of
three vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ as $\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}$ without using brackets.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Note that for any vector $a$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \vec{a} + \vec{0} = \vec{0} + \vec{a} = \vec{a} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here, the zero vector $\vec{0}$ is called the *additive identity* for the vector addition.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.5 Multiplication of a Vector by a Scalar

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $\vec{a}$ be a given vector and $\lambda$ a scalar. Then the product of the vector $\vec{a}$ by the scalar
$\lambda$, denoted as $\lambda\vec{a}$, is called the multiplication of vector $\vec{a}$ by the scalar $\lambda$. Note that, $\lambda\vec{a}$
is also a vector, collinear to the vector $\vec{a}$. The vector $\lambda\vec{a}$ has the direction same (or
opposite) to that of vector $\vec{a}$ according as the value of $\lambda$ is positive (or negative). Also,
the magnitude of vector $\lambda\vec{a}$ is $|\lambda|$ times the magnitude of the vector $\vec{a}$, i.e.,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$|\lambda \vec{a}| = |\lambda| |\vec{a}|$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A geometric visualisation of multiplication of a vector by a scalar is given
in Fig 10.12.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\lambda = -1$, then $\lambda\vec{a} = -\vec{a}$, which is a vector having magnitude equal to the
magnitude of $\vec{a}$ and direction opposite to that of the direction of $\vec{a}$. The vector $-\vec{a}$ is
called the *negative* (or *additive inverse*) of vector $\vec{a}$ and we always have

$$ \vec{a} + (-\vec{a}) = (-\vec{a}) + \vec{a} = \vec{0} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, if $\lambda = \frac{1}{|a|}$, provided $\vec{a} \neq 0$ i.e. $\vec{a}$ is not a null vector, then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$|\lambda \vec{a}| = |\lambda| |\vec{a}| = \frac{1}{|\vec{a}|} |\vec{a}| = 1$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, $\lambda \vec{a}$ represents the unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a}$. We write it as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \hat{a} = \frac{1}{|\vec{a}|} \vec{a} $$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text: Note For any scalar $k$, $k\vec{0} = \vec{0}$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 10.5.1 Components of a vector

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us take the points A(1, 0, 0), B(0, 1, 0) and C(0, 0, 1) on the $x$-axis, $y$-axis and
$z$-axis, respectively. Then, clearly

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$|\overrightarrow{OA}| = 1, |\overrightarrow{OB}| = 1 \text{ and } |\overrightarrow{OC}| = 1$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The vectors $\overline{\text{OA}}$, $\overline{\text{OB}}$ and $\overline{\text{OC}}$, each having magnitude 1,
are called *unit vectors along the axes* OX, OY and OZ,
respectively, and denoted by $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$, respectively
(Fig 10.13).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, consider the position vector $\overline{\text{OP}}$ of a point $\text{P}(x, y, z)$
as in Fig 10.14. Let $\text{P}_1$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $\text{P}$ on the plane XOY.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We, thus, see that $\mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{P}$ is parallel to $z$-axis. As $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ are the unit vectors along the
$x$, $y$ and $z$-axes, respectively, and by the definition of the coordinates of $\mathrm{P}$, we have
$\overline{\mathrm{P}_1 \mathrm{P}} = \overline{\mathrm{OR}} = z \hat{k}$. Similarly, $\overline{\mathrm{QP}_1} = \overline{\mathrm{OS}} = y \hat{j}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{OQ}} = x \hat{i}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, it follows that $\overline{\mathrm{OP}}_{1}=\overline{\mathrm{OQ}}+\overline{\mathrm{QP}}_{1}=x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\overline{\mathrm{OP}} = \overline{\mathrm{OP}_1} + \overline{\mathrm{P}_1\mathrm{P}} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Hence, the position vector of P with reference to O is given by

$$\overline{\mathrm{OP}} (\text{or } \vec{r}) = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
Paragraph
blocks.text:
The length of any vector $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ , is readily determined by applying the
Pythagoras theorem twice. We note that in the right angle triangle $\text{OQP}_1$ (Fig 10.14)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$|\overrightarrow{OP_1}| = \sqrt{|\overrightarrow{OQ}|^2 + |\overrightarrow{QP_1}|^2} = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2},$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: and in the right angle triangle $\text{OP}_1\text{P}$, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\overline{\mathrm{OP}} = \sqrt{|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OP}_1}|^2 + |\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}_1\mathrm{P}}|^2} = \sqrt{(x^2 + y^2) + z^2}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Hence, the length of any vector $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ is given by

$$|\vec{r}| = |x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are any two vectors given in the component form $a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$ and
$b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k}$ , respectively, then

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) the sum (or resultant) of the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is given by
$$\vec{a} + \vec{b} = (a_1 + b_1)\hat{i} + (a_2 + b_2)\hat{j} + (a_3 + b_3)\hat{k}$$
(ii) the difference of the vector $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is given by
$$\vec{a} - \vec{b} = (a_1 - b_1)\hat{i} + (a_2 - b_2)\hat{j} + (a_3 - b_3)\hat{k}$$
(iii) the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are equal if and only if
$$a_1 = b_1, a_2 = b_2 \quad \text{and} \quad a_3 = b_3$$
(iv) the multiplication of vector $\vec{a}$ by any scalar $\lambda$ is given by
$$\lambda\vec{a} = (\lambda a_1)\hat{i} + (\lambda a_2)\hat{j} + (\lambda a_3)\hat{k}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The addition of vectors and the multiplication of a vector by a scalar together give
the following distributive laws:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be any two vectors, and $k$ and $m$ be any scalars. Then

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) $k\vec{a} + m\vec{a} = (k + m)\vec{a}$
(ii) $k(m\vec{a}) = (km)\vec{a}$
(iii) $k(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = k\vec{a} + k\vec{b}$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) One may observe that whatever be the value of $\lambda$, the vector $\lambda \vec{a}$ is always
collinear to the vector $\vec{a}$. In fact, two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are collinear if and only if
there exists a nonzero scalar $\lambda$ such that $\vec{b} = \lambda \vec{a}$. If the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are given
in the component form, i.e. $\vec{a} = a_1 \hat{i} + a_2 \hat{j} + a_3 \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = b_1 \hat{i} + b_2 \hat{j} + b_3 \hat{k}$, then the
two vectors are collinear if and only if

$$b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k} = \lambda(a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k})$$
$$\Leftrightarrow \quad b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k} = (\lambda a_1)\hat{i} + (\lambda a_2)\hat{j} + (\lambda a_3)\hat{k}$$
$$\Leftrightarrow \quad b_1 = \lambda a_1, \ b_2 = \lambda a_2, \ b_3 = \lambda a_3$$
$$\Leftrightarrow \quad \frac{b_1}{a_1} = \frac{b_2}{a_2} = \frac{b_3}{a_3} = \lambda$$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(ii) If $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$, then $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$ are also called direction ratios of $\vec{a}$.

(iii) In case if it is given that $l$, $m$, $n$ are direction cosines of a vector, then $l\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + n\hat{k}$

$= (\cos \alpha)\hat{i} + (\cos \beta)\hat{j} + (\cos \gamma)\hat{k}$ is the unit vector in the direction of that vector,
where $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are the angles which the vector makes with $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes
respectively.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 Find the values of $x$, $y$ and $z$ so that the vectors $\vec{a} = x\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ and
$\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ are equal.

Solution Note that two vectors are equal if and only if their corresponding components
are equal. Thus, the given vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ will be equal if and only if
$$x = 2, y = 2, z = 1$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 5 Let $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j}$. Is $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}|$? Are the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ equal?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Solution We have $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5}$ and $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{2^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{5}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, $|\bar{a}|=|\bar{b}|$. But, the two vectors are not equal since their corresponding components
are distinct.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 6 Find unit vector in the direction of vector $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}$

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Solution The unit vector in the direction of a vector $\vec{a}$ is given by $\hat{a} = \frac{1}{|\vec{a}|} \vec{a}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\hat{a} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}\hat{i} + \frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}\hat{j} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}\hat{k}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 7 Find a vector in the direction of vector $\vec{a} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j}$ that has magnitude
7 units.

Solution The unit vector in the direction of the given vector $\vec{a}$ is

$$ \hat{a} = \frac{1}{|\vec{a}|} \vec{a} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} (\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \hat{i} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \hat{j} $$

Therefore, the vector having magnitude equal to 7 and in the direction of $\vec{a}$ is

$$ 7\hat{a} = 7 \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \hat{i} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \hat{j} \right) = \frac{7}{\sqrt{5}} \hat{i} - \frac{14}{\sqrt{5}} \hat{j} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 8 Find the unit vector in the direction of the sum of the vectors, $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$
and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

Solution The sum of the given vectors is

$$\vec{a} + \vec{b} \text{ (= } \vec{c}, \text{ say}) = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$$

and

$$|\vec{c}| = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{29}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus, the required unit vector is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\hat{c} = \frac{1}{|\vec{c}|} \vec{c} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{29}} (4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) = \frac{4}{\sqrt{29}} \hat{i} + \frac{3}{\sqrt{29}} \hat{j} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{29}} \hat{k}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 9 Write the direction ratio's of the vector $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$ and hence calculate
its direction cosines.

Solution Note that the direction ratio's $a$, $b$, $c$ of a vector $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ are just
the respective components $x$, $y$ and $z$ of the vector. So, for the given vector, we have
$a = 1$, $b = 1$ and $c = -2$. Further, if $l$, $m$ and $n$ are the direction cosines of the given
vector, then

$$1 = \frac{a}{|\vec{r}|} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}, \quad m = \frac{b}{|\vec{r}|} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}, \quad n = \frac{c}{|\vec{r}|} = \frac{-2}{\sqrt{6}} \text{ as } |\vec{r}| = \sqrt{6}$$

Thus, the direction cosines are $\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}, -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \right)$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 10.5.2 Vector joining two points

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $\mathrm{P}_1(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $\mathrm{P}_2(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ are any two
points, then the vector joining $\mathrm{P}_1$ and $\mathrm{P}_2$ is the
vector $\overline{\mathrm{P}_1\mathrm{P}_2}$ (Fig 10.15).

Joining the points $\mathrm{P}_1$ and $\mathrm{P}_2$ with the origin
O, and applying triangle law, from the triangle
$\mathrm{OP}_1\mathrm{P}_2$, we have

$$ \overrightarrow{OP_1} + \overrightarrow{P_1P_2} = \overrightarrow{OP_2} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Using the properties of vector addition, the
above equation becomes

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\overline{P_1 P_2} = \overline{OP_2} - \overline{OP_1}$$

i.e. $\overline{\mathrm{P}_1\mathrm{P}_2} = (x_2\hat{i} + y_2\hat{j} + z_2\hat{k}) - (x_1\hat{i} + y_1\hat{j} + z_1\hat{k})$
$= (x_2 - x_1)\hat{i} + (y_2 - y_1)\hat{j} + (z_2 - z_1)\hat{k}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The magnitude of vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}_1\mathrm{P}_2}$ is given by

$$|\overrightarrow{P_1 P_2}| = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 10 Find the vector joining the points $P(2, 3, 0)$ and $Q(- 1, - 2, - 4)$ directed
from $P$ to $Q$.

Solution Since the vector is to be directed from $P$ to $Q$, clearly $P$ is the initial point
and $Q$ is the terminal point. So, the required vector joining $P$ and $Q$ is the vector $\overline{PQ}$,
given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\overline{\mathrm{PQ}} = (-1-2)\hat{i} + (-2-3)\hat{j} + (-4-0)\hat{k}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e. $\overline{\mathrm{PQ}} = -3\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}.$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 10.5.3 Section formula

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let P and Q be two points represented by the position vectors $\overline{\text{OP}}$ and $\overline{\text{OQ}}$, respectively,
with respect to the origin O. Then the line segment
joining the points P and Q may be divided by a third
point, say R, in two ways – internally (Fig 10.16)
and externally (Fig 10.17). Here, we intend to find
the position vector $\overline{\text{OR}}$ for the point R with respect
to the origin O. We take the two cases one by one.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Case I When R divides PQ internally (Fig 10.16).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If R divides $\overline{\mathrm{PQ}}$ such that $m \overline{\mathrm{RQ}} = n \overline{\mathrm{PR}}$,

where $m$ and $n$ are positive scalars, we say that the point R divides $\overline{\text{PQ}}$ internally in the
ratio of $m : n$. Now from triangles ORQ and OPR, we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\overline{\mathrm{RQ}} = \overline{\mathrm{OQ}} - \overline{\mathrm{OR}} = \vec{b} - \vec{r}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $\overline{\mathrm{PR}} = \overline{\mathrm{OR}} - \overline{\mathrm{OP}} = \vec{r} - \vec{a},$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, we have $m(\vec{b}-\vec{r})=n(\vec{r}-\vec{a})$ (Why?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or $\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \vec{r} = \frac{m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}}{m + n} \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{(on simplification)}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Hence, the position vector of the point R which divides P and Q internally in the
ratio of $m : n$ is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{OR}} = \frac{m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}}{m + n} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case II When R divides PQ externally (Fig 10.17).
We leave it to the reader as an exercise to verify
that the position vector of the point R which divides
the line segment PQ externally in the ratio

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$m:n \quad \text{i.e.} \quad \frac{\text{PR}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{m}{n} \quad \text{is given by}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{OR}} = \frac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\textit{\textbf{Remark}}$ If R is the midpoint of PQ , then $m = n$. And therefore, from Case I, the
midpoint R of $\overline{\text{PQ}}$, will have its position vector as

$$\overline{\text{OR}} = \frac{\vec{a} + \vec{b}}{2}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 11 Consider two points P and Q with position vectors $\overrightarrow{\text{OP}} = 3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}$ and
$\overrightarrow{\text{OQ}} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$. Find the position vector of a point R which divides the line joining P and Q
in the ratio 2:1, (i) internally, and (ii) externally.

Solution

(i) The position vector of the point R dividing the join of P and Q internally in the
ratio 2:1 is
$$\overrightarrow{\text{OR}} = \frac{2(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) + (3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b})}{2 + 1} = \frac{5\vec{a}}{3}$$
(ii) The position vector of the point R dividing the join of P and Q externally in the
ratio 2:1 is
$$\overrightarrow{\text{OR}} = \frac{2(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) - (3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b})}{2 - 1} = 4\vec{b} - \vec{a}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 12 Show that the points A($2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$), B($\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$), C($3\hat{i} - 4j - 4\hat{k}$) are
the vertices of a right angled triangle.

Solution We have
$$\overline{\text{AB}} = (1-2)\hat{i} + (-3+1)\hat{j} + (-5-1)\hat{k} = -\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$$
$$\overline{\text{BC}} = (3-1)\hat{i} + (-4+3)\hat{j} + (-4+5)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$$
and $$\overline{\text{CA}} = (2-3)\hat{i} + (-1+4)\hat{j} + (1+4)\hat{k} = -\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$$
flags: [translation_divergence] The Hindi version uses a different vector font representation for C ($3\hat{i} - 4j - 4\hat{k}$) where 'j' lacks a hat symbol in the Hindi source text as well, which might be an OCR error or a slight typography mismatch.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Further, note that

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2 = 41 = 6 + 35 = |\overrightarrow{BC}|^2 + |\overrightarrow{CA}|^2$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the triangle is a right angled triangle.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.6 Product of Two Vectors

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So far we have studied about addition and subtraction of vectors. An other algebraic
operation which we intend to discuss regarding vectors is their product. We may
recall that product of two numbers is a number, product of two matrices is again a
matrix. But in case of functions, we may multiply them in two ways, namely,
multiplication of two functions pointwise and composition of two functions. Similarly,
multiplication of two vectors is also defined in two ways, namely, scalar (or dot)
product where the result is a scalar, and vector (or cross) product where the
result is a vector. Based upon these two types of products for vectors, they have
found various applications in geometry, mechanics and engineering. In this section,
we will discuss these two types of products.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 10.6.1 Scalar (or dot) product of two vectors

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Definition 2 The scalar product of two nonzero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, denoted by $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$, is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: defined as $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \cos\theta,$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where, $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (Fig 10.19).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If either $\vec{a}=0$ or $\vec{b}=0$ then $\theta$ is not defined, and in this case, we

define $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}=0$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Observations

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is a real number.
2. Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two nonzero vectors, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$ if and only if $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are
perpendicular to each other. i.e.
$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0 \Leftrightarrow \vec{a} \perp \vec{b}$
3. If $\theta = 0$, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|$
In particular, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$, as $\theta$ in this case is 0.
4. If $\theta = \pi$, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = -|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|$
In particular, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = -|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|$, as $\theta$ in this case is $\pi$.
5. In view of the Observations 2 and 3, for mutually perpendicular unit vectors
$\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$, we have
$$\hat{i} \cdot \hat{i} = \hat{j} \cdot \hat{j} = \hat{k} \cdot \hat{k} = 1,$$
$$\hat{i} \cdot \hat{j} = \hat{j} \cdot \hat{k} = \hat{k} \cdot \hat{i} = 0$$
6. The angle between two nonzero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is given by
$$\cos \theta = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|}, \text{ or } \theta = \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|} \right)$$
7. The scalar product is commutative. i.e.

blocks.text: $$ \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} \qquad (\text{Why?}) $$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Two important properties of scalar product

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Property 1 (Distributivity of scalar product over addition) Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be
any three vectors, then

$$ \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: \textbf{Property 2} Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be any two vectors, and l be any scalar. Then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$(\lambda\vec{a})\cdot\vec{b} = (\lambda\vec{a})\cdot\vec{b} = \lambda(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}) = \vec{a}\cdot(\lambda\vec{b})$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are given in component form as $a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$ and
$b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k}$ , then their scalar product is given as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \begin{aligned} \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} &= (a_1 \hat{i} + a_2 \hat{j} + a_3 \hat{k}) \cdot (b_1 \hat{i} + b_2 \hat{j} + b_3 \hat{k}) \\ &= a_1 \hat{i} \cdot (b_1 \hat{i} + b_2 \hat{j} + b_3 \hat{k}) + a_2 \hat{j} \cdot (b_1 \hat{i} + b_2 \hat{j} + b_3 \hat{k}) + a_3 \hat{k} \cdot (b_1 \hat{i} + b_2 \hat{j} + b_3 \hat{k}) \\ &= a_1 b_1 (\hat{i} \cdot \hat{i}) + a_1 b_2 (\hat{i} \cdot \hat{j}) + a_1 b_3 (\hat{i} \cdot \hat{k}) + a_2 b_1 (\hat{j} \cdot \hat{i}) + a_2 b_2 (\hat{j} \cdot \hat{j}) + a_2 b_3 (\hat{j} \cdot \hat{k}) \\ &\quad + a_3 b_1 (\hat{k} \cdot \hat{i}) + a_3 b_2 (\hat{k} \cdot \hat{j}) + a_3 b_3 (\hat{k} \cdot \hat{k}) \text{ (Using the above Properties 1 and 2)} \\ &= a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3 \end{aligned} \quad \text{(Using Observation 5)} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Thus

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 10.6.2 Projection of a vector on a line

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose a vector $\overline{\text{AB}}$ makes an angle $\theta$ with a given directed line $l$ (say), in the
anticlockwise direction (Fig 10.20). Then the projection of $\overline{\text{AB}}$ on $l$ is a vector $\vec{p}$
(say) with magnitude $|\overline{\text{AB}}|$ $|\cos \theta|$, and the direction of $\vec{p}$ being the same (or opposite)
to that of the line $l$, depending upon whether $\cos \theta$ is positive or negative. The vector $\vec{p}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
is called the *projection vector*, and its magnitude $|\bar{p}|$ is simply called as the *projection*
of the vector $\overline{\text{AB}}$ on the directed line $l$.

For example, in each of the following figures (Fig 10.20 (i) to (iv)), projection vector
of $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AB}}$ along the line $l$ is vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AC}}$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Observations

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. If $\hat{p}$ is the unit vector along a line $l$, then the projection of a vector $\vec{a}$ on the line
$l$ is given by $\vec{a} \cdot \hat{p}$ .

2. Projection of a vector $\vec{a}$ on other vector $\vec{b}$, is given by

$$\vec{a} \cdot \hat{b}, \quad \text{or} \quad \vec{a} \cdot \left( \frac{\vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} \right), \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{1}{|\vec{b}|} (\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})$$

3. If $\theta = 0$, then the projection vector of $\overline{\text{AB}}$ will be $\overline{\text{AB}}$ itself and if $\theta = \pi$, then the
projection vector of $\overline{\text{AB}}$ will be $\overline{\text{BA}}$.

4. If $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ or $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$, then the projection vector of $\overline{\text{AB}}$ will be zero vector.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
$\textit{Remark}$ If $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are the direction angles of vector $\vec{a} = a_1 \hat{i} + a_2 \hat{j} + a_3 \hat{k}$ , then its
direction cosines may be given as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\cos \alpha = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \hat{i}}{|\vec{a}||\hat{i}|} = \frac{a_1}{|\vec{a}|}, \cos \beta = \frac{a_2}{|\vec{a}|}, \text{ and } \cos \gamma = \frac{a_3}{|\vec{a}|}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Also, note that $|\vec{a}|\cos\alpha$, $|\vec{a}|\cos\beta$ and $|\vec{a}|\cos\gamma$ are respectively the projections of
$\vec{a}$ along OX, OY and OZ. i.e., the scalar components $a_1$, $a_2$ and $a_3$ of the vector $\vec{a}$, are
precisely the projections of $\vec{a}$ along $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis, respectively. Further, if $\vec{a}$
is a unit vector, then it may be expressed in terms of its direction cosines as

$$ \vec{a} = \cos \alpha \hat{i} + \cos \beta \hat{j} + \cos \gamma \hat{k} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 13 Find the angle between two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ with magnitudes 1 and 2
respectively and when $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 1$.

Solution Given $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 1, |\vec{a}| = 1$ and $|\vec{b}| = 2$ . We have

$$\theta = \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|} \right) = \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{2} \right) = \frac{\pi}{3}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 14 Find angle ‘$\theta$’ between the vectors $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$.


Solution The angle $\theta$ between two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is given by


$$\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}$$


Now $$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = (\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}) \cdot (\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1.$$


Therefore, we have $$\cos\theta = \frac{-1}{3}$$


hence the required angle is $$\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)$$

Example 15 If $\vec{a}=5\hat{i}-\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-5\hat{k}$, then show that the vectors
$\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}-\vec{b}$ are perpendicular.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution We know that two nonzero vectors are perpendicular if their scalar product
is zero.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Here $\quad \bar{a}+\bar{b}=(5 \hat{i}-\hat{j}-3 \hat{k})+(\hat{i}+3 \hat{j}-5 \hat{k})=6 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-8 \hat{k}$

and $\quad \bar{a}-\bar{b}=(5 \hat{i}-\hat{j}-3 \hat{k})-(\hat{i}+3 \hat{j}-5 \hat{k})=4 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$

So $\quad(\bar{a}+\bar{b}) \cdot(\bar{a}-\bar{b})=(6 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-8 \hat{k}) \cdot(4 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}+2 \hat{k})=24-8-16=0$.

Hence $\quad \bar{a}+\bar{b}$ and $\bar{a}-\bar{b}$ are perpendicular vectors.

$\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

Solution The projection of vector $\vec{a}$ on the vector $\vec{b}$ is given by

$$\frac{1}{|\vec{b}|}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) = \frac{(2 \times 1 + 3 \times 2 + 2 \times 1)}{\sqrt{(1)^2 + (2)^2 + (1)^2}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{6}} = \frac{5}{3}\sqrt{6}$$

and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 4$.

$$|\vec{a} - \vec{b}|^2 = (\vec{a} - \vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a} - \vec{b})$$
$$= \vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} - \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} - \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} + \vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \begin{aligned} &= |\vec{a}|^2 - 2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) + |\vec{b}|^2 \\ &= (2)^2 - 2(4) + (3)^2 \end{aligned} $$

Therefore $|\vec{a} - \vec{b}| = \sqrt{5}$

Therefore $$|\vec{x}| = 3 \text{ (as magnitude of a vector is non negative).}$$

blocks.text:
Example 20 For any two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, we always
have $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| \le |\vec{a}| + |\vec{b}|$ (triangle inequality).

Solution The inequality holds trivially in case either
$\vec{a} = \vec{0}$ or $\vec{b} = \vec{0}$ (How?). So, let $|\vec{a}| \neq \vec{0} \neq |\vec{b}|$. Then,
$$|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2 = (\vec{a} + \vec{b})^2 = (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a} + \vec{b})$$
$$= \vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} + \vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}$$
$$= |\vec{a}|^2 + 2|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}| + |\vec{b}|^2 \quad \text{(scalar product is commutative)}$$
$$\le |\vec{a}|^2 + 2|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}| + |\vec{b}|^2 \quad \text{(since } x \le |x| \ \forall x \in \mathbf{R} \text{ )}$$
$$\le |\vec{a}|^2 + 2|\vec{a}||\vec{b}| + |\vec{b}|^2 \quad \text{(from Example 19)}$$

$$\overline{BC} = (7-1)\hat{i} + (0-2)\hat{j} + (-1-3)\hat{k} = 6\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k} ,$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: 10.6.3 Vector (or cross) product of two vectors

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Section 10.2, we have discussed on the three dimensional right handed rectangular
coordinate system. In this system, when the positive $x$-axis is rotated counterclockwise

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
into the positive $y$-axis, a right handed (standard) screw would advance in the direction
of the positive $z$-axis (Fig 10.22(i)).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In a right handed coordinate system, the thumb of the right hand points in the
direction of the positive $z$-axis when the fingers are curled in the direction away from
the positive $x$-axis toward the positive $y$-axis (Fig 10.22(ii)).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Definition 3 The vector product of two nonzero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, is denoted by $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$
and defined as

$$ \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin \theta \hat{n} , $$

where, $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ and $\hat{n}$ is a
unit vector perpendicular to both $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, such that
$\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\hat{n}$ form a right handed system (Fig 10.23). i.e., the
right handed system rotated from $\vec{a}$ to $\vec{b}$ moves in the direction
of $\hat{n}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: If either $\vec{a} = \vec{0}$ or $\vec{b} = \vec{0}$ , then $\theta$ is not defined and in this case, we define $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}$ .

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Observations

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is a vector.

2. Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two nonzero vectors. Then $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0}$ if and only if $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are
parallel (or collinear) to each other, i.e.,

$$ \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \vec{0} \Leftrightarrow \vec{a} \| \vec{b} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In particular, $\vec{a} \times \vec{a} = \vec{0}$ and $\vec{a} \times (-\vec{a}) = \vec{0}$, since in the first situation, $\theta = 0$ and
in the second one, $\theta = \pi$, making the value of $\sin \theta$ to be 0.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: 3. If $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ then $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|$.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
4. In view of the Observations 2 and 3, for mutually perpendicular
unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ (Fig 10.24), we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \hat{i} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k} \times \hat{k} = \vec{0} $$

$$ \hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}, \quad \hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}, \quad \hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} $$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
5. In terms of vector product, the angle between two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ may be
given as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin \theta = \frac{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}{|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|} $$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
6. It is always true that the vector product is not commutative, as $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = -\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$.
Indeed, $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin \theta \hat{n}$, where $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\hat{n}$ form a right handed system,
i.e., $\theta$ is traversed from $\vec{a}$ to $\vec{b}$, Fig 10.25 (i). While, $\vec{b} \times \vec{a} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin \theta \hat{n}_1$, where
$\vec{b}, \vec{a}$ and $\hat{n}_1$ form a right handed system i.e. $\theta$ is traversed from $\vec{b}$ to $\vec{a}$ ,
Fig 10.25(ii).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, if we assume $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ to lie in the plane of the paper, then $\hat{n}$ and $\hat{n}_1$ both
will be perpendicular to the plane of the paper. But, $\hat{n}$ being directed above the
paper while $\hat{n}_1$ directed below the paper. i.e. $\hat{n}_1 = -\hat{n}$ .

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Hence $\qquad \qquad \qquad \bar{a} \times \bar{b} = |\bar{a}| |\bar{b}| \sin \theta \hat{n}$
$\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad = -|\bar{a}| |\bar{b}| \sin \theta \hat{n}_1 = -\bar{b} \times \bar{a}$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
7. In view of the Observations 4 and 6, we have
$$\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}, \quad \hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i} \text{ and } \quad \hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}.$$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
8. If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ represent the adjacent sides of a triangle then its area is given as

$$\frac{1}{2} |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| .$$

By definition of the area of a triangle, we have from
Fig 10.26,

$$ \text{Area of triangle ABC} = \frac{1}{2} \text{AB} \cdot \text{CD}. $$

But $AB = |\vec{b}|$ (as given), and $CD = |\vec{a}| \sin \theta.$

Thus, Area of triangle ABC = $\frac{1}{2}|\vec{b}||\vec{a}|\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}|.$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
9. If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ represent the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, then its area is given
by $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From Fig 10.27, we have
Area of parallelogram ABCD = AB. DE.
But AB = $|\vec{b}|$ (as given), and
DE = $|\vec{a}| \sin \theta$.
Thus,
Area of parallelogram ABCD = $|\vec{b}| |\vec{a}| \sin \theta = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$.
We now state two important properties of vector product.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Property 3 (Distributivity of vector product over addition): If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$
are any three vectors and $\lambda$ be a scalar, then

(i) $\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \times \vec{b} + \vec{a} \times \vec{c}$

(ii) $\lambda(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) = (\lambda \vec{a}) \times \vec{b} = \vec{a} \times (\lambda \vec{b})$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be two vectors given in component form as $a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$ and
$b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k}$ , respectively. Then their cross product may be given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Explanation We have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \begin{aligned} \vec{a} \times \vec{b} &= (a_1 \hat{i} + a_2 \hat{j} + a_3 \hat{k}) \times (b_1 \hat{i} + b_2 \hat{j} + b_3 \hat{k}) \\ &= a_1 b_1 (\hat{i} \times \hat{i}) + a_1 b_2 (\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) + a_1 b_3 (\hat{i} \times \hat{k}) + a_2 b_1 (\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) \\ &\quad + a_2 b_2 (\hat{j} \times \hat{j}) + a_2 b_3 (\hat{j} \times \hat{k}) \\ &\quad + a_3 b_1 (\hat{k} \times \hat{i}) + a_3 b_2 (\hat{k} \times \hat{j}) + a_3 b_3 (\hat{k} \times \hat{k}) \end{aligned} \text{ (by Property 1)} $$
$$ = a_1 b_2 (\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) - a_1 b_3 (\hat{k} \times \hat{i}) - a_2 b_1 (\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) $$
$$ \quad + a_2 b_3 (\hat{j} \times \hat{k}) + a_3 b_1 (\hat{k} \times \hat{i}) - a_3 b_2 (\hat{j} \times \hat{k}) $$
$$ (\text{as } \hat{i} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k} \times \hat{k} = 0 \text{ and } \hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{k} \times \hat{i}, \hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{i} \times \hat{j} \text{ and } \hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{j} \times \hat{k}) $$
$$ = a_1 b_2 \hat{k} - a_1 b_3 \hat{j} - a_2 b_1 \hat{k} + a_2 b_3 \hat{i} + a_3 b_1 \hat{j} - a_3 b_2 \hat{i} $$
$$ (\text{as } \hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}, \hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i} \text{ and } \hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}) $$
$$ = (a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2) \hat{i} - (a_1 b_3 - a_3 b_1) \hat{j} + (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1) \hat{k} $$
$$ \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 22 Find $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$, if $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$

Solution We have

$$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \end{vmatrix}$$

$$= \hat{i}(-2 - 15) - (-4 - 9)\hat{j} + (10 - 3)\hat{k} = -17\hat{i} + 13\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}$$

Hence $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = \sqrt{(-17)^2 + (13)^2 + (7)^2} = \sqrt{507}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 23 Find a unit vector perpendicular to each of the vectors $(\vec{a}+\vec{b})$ and


$(\vec{a}-\vec{b})$, where $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$.

Solution We have $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = -\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$

A vector which is perpendicular to both $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ and $\vec{a} - \vec{b}$ is given by

$$ (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a} - \vec{b}) = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = -2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k} \quad (\text{= } \vec{c}, \text{ say}) $$

Now $|\vec{c}| = \sqrt{4+16+4} = \sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6}$

Therefore, the required unit vector is

$$ \frac{\vec{c}}{|\vec{c}|} = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{i} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{j} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{k} $$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Note There are two perpendicular directions to any plane. Thus, another unit
vector perpendicular to $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ and $\vec{a} - \vec{b}$ will be $\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{i} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{j} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\hat{k}$. But that will
be a consequence of $(\vec{a} - \vec{b}) \times (\vec{a} + \vec{b})$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 24 Find the area of a triangle having the points A(1, 1, 1), B(1, 2, 3)
and C(2, 3, 1) as its vertices.

Solution We have $\overline{\text{AB}} = \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\overline{\text{AC}} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$. The area of the given triangle
is $\frac{1}{2} |\overline{\text{AB}} \times \overline{\text{AC}}|$.

Now, $\overline{\text{AB}} \times \overline{\text{AC}} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$

Therefore $|\overline{\text{AB}} \times \overline{\text{AC}}| = \sqrt{16 + 4 + 1} = \sqrt{21}$

Thus, the required area is $\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{21}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 25 Find the area of a parallelogram whose adjacent sides are given
by the vectors $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution The area of a parallelogram with $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ as its adjacent sides is given
by $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now $\bar{a} \times \bar{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 5\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = \sqrt{25+1+16} = \sqrt{42}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: and hence, the required area is $\sqrt{42}$.

blocks.text: Example 26 Write all the unit vectors in XY-plane.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution Let $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j}$ be a unit vector in XY-plane (Fig 10.28). Then, from the
figure, we have $x = \cos \theta$ and $y = \sin \theta$ (since $|\vec{r}| = 1$). So, we may write the vector $\vec{r}$ as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\vec{r}(=\overline{\text{OP}}) = \cos \theta \hat{i} + \sin \theta \hat{j} \quad \dots (1)$$
Clearly,
$$|\vec{r}| = \sqrt{\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta} = 1$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Also, as $\theta$ varies from 0 to $2\pi$, the point P (Fig 10.28) traces the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$
counterclockwise, and this covers all possible directions. So, (1) gives every unit vector
in the XY-plane.

Example 27 If $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}$, $3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ are the position
vectors of points A, B, C and D respectively, then find the angle between $\overline{\text{AB}}$ and $\overline{\text{CD}}$.
Deduce that $\overline{\text{AB}}$ and $\overline{\text{CD}}$ are collinear.
flags: [translation_divergence] English mentions 'angle between \overline{\text{AB}} and \overline{\text{CD}}', whereas Hindi translates it as 'सरल रेखाओं AB तथा CD के बीच का कोण' (angle between straight lines AB and CD).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution Note that if $\theta$ is the angle between AB and CD, then $\theta$ is also the angle
between $\overline{\text{AB}}$ and $\overline{\text{CD}}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now $\overline{\text{AB}} =$ Position vector of B – Position vector of A
$= (2\hat{i} + 5\hat{j}) - (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - \hat{k}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $$\|\overline{\mathrm{AB}}\| = \sqrt{(1)^2 + (4)^2 + (-1)^2} = 3\sqrt{2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly $\overline{\mathrm{CD}} = -2\hat{i} - 8\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $|\overline{\mathrm{CD}}| = 6\sqrt{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Thus $\cos \theta = \frac{\overline{\text{AB}} \cdot \overline{\text{CD}}}{|\overline{\text{AB}}||\overline{\text{CD}}|}$
$= \frac{1(-2) + 4(-8) + (-1)(2)}{(3\sqrt{2})(6\sqrt{2})} = \frac{-36}{36} = -1$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Since $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$, it follows that $\theta = \pi$. This shows that $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{CD}}$ are collinear.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Alternatively, $\overline{\text{AB}} = -\frac{1}{2}\overline{\text{CD}}$ which implies that $\overline{\text{AB}}$ and $\overline{\text{CD}}$ are collinear vectors.

Example 28 Let $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three vectors such that $|\vec{a}|=3, |\vec{b}|=4, |\vec{c}|=5$ and

each one of them being perpendicular to the sum of the other two, find $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution Given $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = 0$, $\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{c} + \vec{a}) = 0$, $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = 0$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now
$$|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^2=(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})^2=(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})\cdot(\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c})$$
$$=\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}+\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}+\vec{c})+\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}+\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{a}+\vec{c})$$
$$+\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{a}+\vec{b})+\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}$$
$$=|\vec{a}|^2+|\vec{b}|^2+|\vec{c}|^2$$
$$=9+16+25=50$$
Therefore
$$|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c} = \vec{0} = 0 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore $\quad \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} = -|\vec{a}|^2 = -9 \quad \dots (1)$

blocks.label: Equation

blocks.label: Equation

blocks.label: Equation

Summary

Position vector of a point P(x, y, z) is given as $\overline{\text{OP}}(=\bar{r}) = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$, and its
magnitude by $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}$ .
The scalar components of a vector are its direction ratios, and represent its
projections along the respective axes.
The magnitude (r), direction ratios (a, b, c) and direction cosines (l, m, n) of
any vector are related as:

$$l = \frac{a}{r}, \quad m = \frac{b}{r}, \quad n = \frac{c}{r}$$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
The vector sum of the three sides of a triangle taken in order is $\vec{0}$.
The vector sum of two coinitial vectors is given by the diagonal of the
parallelogram whose adjacent sides are the given vectors.
The multiplication of a given vector by a scalar $\lambda$, changes the magnitude of
the vector by the multiple $|\lambda|$, and keeps the direction same (or makes it
opposite) according as the value of $\lambda$ is positive (or negative).

For a given vector $\vec{a}$, the vector $\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$ gives the unit vector in the direction
of $\vec{a}$.
The position vector of a point R dividing a line segment joining the points
P and Q whose position vectors are $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ respectively, in the ratio $m : n$

(i) internally, is given by $\frac{n\vec{a} + m\vec{b}}{m + n}$.

(ii) externally, is given by $\frac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n}$.

The scalar product of two given vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ having angle $\theta$ between
them is defined as
$$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \cos \theta.$$
Also, when $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is given, the angle '$\theta$' between the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ may be
determined by
$$\cos \theta = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|}$$

If $\theta$ is the angle between two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, then their cross product is
given as
$$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin \theta \hat{n}$$
where $\hat{n}$ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$. Such
that $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \hat{n}$ form right handed system of coordinate axes.

If we have two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, given in component form as
$\vec{a} = a_1 \hat{i} + a_2 \hat{j} + a_3 \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = b_1 \hat{i} + b_2 \hat{j} + b_3 \hat{k}$ and $\lambda$ any scalar,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
then $\quad \bar{a}+\bar{b}=\left(a_{1}+b_{1}\right) \hat{i}+\left(a_{2}+b_{2}\right) \hat{j}+\left(a_{3}+b_{3}\right) \hat{k} ;$

$\lambda \bar{a}=\left(\lambda a_{1}\right) \hat{i}+\left(\lambda a_{2}\right) \hat{j}+\left(\lambda a_{3}\right) \hat{k} ;$

$\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}=a_{1} b_{1}+a_{2} b_{2}+a_{3} b_{3} ;$

and $\quad \bar{a} \times \bar{b}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_{1} & b_{1} & c_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} & c_{2} \end{array}\right| .$

Historical Note

The word vector has been derived from a Latin word vectus, which means
“to carry”. The germinal ideas of modern vector theory date from around 1800
when Caspar Wessel (1745-1818) and Jean Robert Argand (1768-1822) described
that how a complex number $a + ib$ could be given a geometric interpretation with
the help of a directed line segment in a coordinate plane. William Rowen Hamilton
(1805-1865) an Irish mathematician was the first to use the term vector for a
directed line segment in his book Lectures on Quaternions (1853). Hamilton’s
method of quaternions (an ordered set of four real numbers given as:
$a + b\hat{i} + c\hat{j} + d\hat{k}, \hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ following certain algebraic rules) was a solution to the
problem of multiplying vectors in three dimensional space. Though, we must
mention here that in practice, the idea of vector concept and their addition was
known much earlier ever since the time of Aristotle (384-322 B.C.), a Greek
philosopher, and pupil of Plato (427-348 B.C.). That time it was supposed to be
known that the combined action of two or more forces could be seen by adding
them according to parallelogram law. The correct law for the composition of
forces, that forces add vectorially, had been discovered in the case of perpendicular
forces by Stevin-Simon (1548-1620). In 1586 A.D., he analysed the principle of
geometric addition of forces in his treatise DeBeghinelen der Weeghconst
(“Principles of the Art of Weighing”), which caused a major breakthrough in the
development of mechanics. But it took another 200 years for the general concept
of vectors to form.

In the 1880, Josiah Willard Gibbs (1839-1903), an American physicist and
mathematician, and Oliver Heaviside (1850-1925), an English engineer, created
what we now know as vector analysis, essentially by separating the real (scalar)
